lesson.title: Python Fundamentals: Types, Variables and Control Flow
objectives: Explain how Python variables work as names bound to objects.
Distinguish mutable and immutable built-in types and why it matters.
Use if/elif/else, for, while, break, continue and the loop else clause correctly.
Explain truthiness, the difference between == and is, and integer vs float division.
Write a small stdin/stdout program that combines input parsing, branching and loops.
lesson.definition: Python is a dynamically typed, strongly typed, interpreted language. A variable is a name that refers to an object; the object, not the name, carries the type. Control flow statements (if, for, while) decide which code runs and how many times, using indentation to mark blocks.

theory.heading: Names, objects and dynamic typing
theory.body: In Python every value is an object with an identity, a type and a value. An assignment such as x = 10 does not put 10 into a box called x; it binds the name x to an int object. Rebinding x = 'ten' simply points the name at a different object. That is dynamic typing. Python is still strongly typed: '3' + 4 raises TypeError instead of silently converting, unlike JavaScript.
points: type(x) returns the class of the object the name refers to.
id(x) returns the object's identity; two names can share one object.
Strong typing means no implicit conversion between unrelated types.
Type hints (x: int = 5) document intent but are not enforced at runtime.

theory.heading: Built-in types and mutability
theory.body: The core scalar types are int (arbitrary precision), float (IEEE 754 double), complex, bool (a subclass of int) and NoneType. Sequence and collection types are str, list, tuple, dict and set. The key interview distinction is mutability: immutable objects (int, float, str, tuple, frozenset) cannot change after creation, so an operation that looks like modification creates a new object. Mutable objects (list, dict, set) change in place, which matters when two names share the same object.
points: Immutable: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes.
Mutable: list, dict, set, bytearray and most user-defined objects.
Only hashable (normally immutable) objects can be dict keys or set members.
0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 because of binary floating point; use decimal.Decimal for money.

theory.heading: Operators that interviewers probe
theory.body: / always returns a float (7 / 2 == 3.5), // is floor division (7 // 2 == 3, and -7 // 2 == -4 because it floors toward negative infinity) and % follows the sign of the divisor. == compares values by calling __eq__, while is compares identity. Use is only for singletons such as None. and/or short-circuit and return one of their operands, not necessarily a bool: '' or 'guest' evaluates to 'guest'.
points: x is None is the idiomatic None check.
Chained comparisons work: 0 <= score <= 100.
Falsy values: None, False, 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, set(), range(0).
The walrus operator := assigns inside an expression (Python 3.8+).

theory.heading: Control flow
theory.body: if/elif/else picks one branch. for iterates over any iterable (lists, strings, dicts, files, ranges); while repeats while a condition is true. break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration, and the optional else block on a loop runs only if the loop finished without break, which is handy for search loops. Python 3.10 added match/case for structural pattern matching.
points: range(start, stop, step) is lazy and excludes stop.
enumerate(items, start=1) gives index and value together.
zip(a, b) walks two iterables in parallel and stops at the shorter one.
Indentation is syntax: mixing tabs and spaces causes errors.

theory.heading: Strings and input handling
theory.body: Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode characters. Common methods are strip, split, join, replace, lower, startswith and format with f-strings. input() always returns a str, so numeric input must be converted with int() or float(). f'{value:.2f}' formats a float with two decimals, which you will use constantly in coding rounds.
points: s.split() with no argument splits on any whitespace and drops empty parts.
', '.join(words) is the efficient way to build a string from pieces.
Slicing s[::-1] reverses a string; slices never raise IndexError.

example.title: Mutability in action
example.body: Two names bound to the same list see each other's changes, while rebinding an int creates a new object. This is the root of many subtle bugs, such as a function unexpectedly modifying a list it received.

code.source:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            # b and a refer to the SAME list
b.append(4)
print(a)         # [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(a is b)    # True

x = 10
y = x
y += 1           # ints are immutable: y now refers to a new object
print(x, y)      # 10 11

c = a[:]         # shallow copy creates a new list
print(c == a, c is a)  # True False

Python is dynamically but strongly typed.
Know which types are mutable; it affects copying, defaults and dict keys.
Use == for value equality and is only for identity checks like is None.
/ returns float, // floors toward negative infinity.
A loop's else block runs only when the loop was not exited with break.

interview.question: Is Python statically or dynamically typed? Strongly or weakly typed?
interview.answer: Dynamically typed, because types are checked at runtime and a name can be rebound to an object of any type. Strongly typed, because it does not implicitly convert between unrelated types; '3' + 4 raises TypeError.
interview.explanation: Many candidates confuse dynamic with weak. Giving the '3' + 4 example and contrasting it with JavaScript's '34' shows you understand both axes.

interview.question: What is the difference between == and is?
interview.answer: == compares values using __eq__; is compares identity, meaning both names point to the same object. Use is for singletons such as None, True and False.
interview.explanation: Mention that small integers and some strings are cached by CPython, so is may appear to work for them, but relying on that is a bug.

interview.question: Which built-in types are mutable and which are immutable? Why does it matter?
interview.answer: Mutable: list, dict, set, bytearray. Immutable: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes. It matters because shared references to mutable objects see in-place changes, and only hashable objects can be dictionary keys or set members.
interview.explanation: A strong answer connects mutability to real consequences: aliasing bugs, the mutable default argument trap and hashability.

interview.question: What does the else clause on a for or while loop do?
interview.answer: It runs after the loop finishes normally, that is, without hitting break. It is useful for search loops where you need to act when nothing was found.
interview.explanation: This is a classic Python-specific question; a short search example demonstrates you have actually used it.

interview.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 return False, and how do you handle money in Python?
interview.answer: Floats are binary IEEE 754 doubles and cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. For money use decimal.Decimal (constructed from strings) or store integer paise/cents; for approximate comparisons use math.isclose.
interview.explanation: Interviewers for full-stack roles like this because payment and invoice code must avoid float rounding errors; Django's DecimalField exists for the same reason.

lesson.title: Functions, Arguments, Scope and Closures
objectives: Define functions with positional, keyword, default, *args and **kwargs parameters.
Explain the LEGB scope rule and when global and nonlocal are needed.
Avoid the mutable default argument trap and explain why it happens.
Use functions as first-class objects: pass them, return them and store them in dicts.
Build closures and lambdas and know their limits.
lesson.definition: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def that takes parameters and returns a value (None if no return runs). In Python functions are first-class objects, so they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments and returned from other functions; a closure is a nested function that remembers variables from the scope in which it was created.

theory.heading: Parameters and arguments
theory.body: Parameters are the names in the def line; arguments are the values passed in a call. Python matches arguments in a fixed order: positional, then keyword. *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. A bare * in the signature makes the following parameters keyword-only, and / (Python 3.8+) makes the preceding ones positional-only. Clear signatures make APIs harder to misuse.
points: def f(a, b=2, *args, flag=False, **kwargs) is a valid full signature.
f(*items) unpacks a list into positional arguments; f(**opts) unpacks a dict into keywords.
Keyword-only parameters (after *) force callers to write send(to=..., cc=...).
A function without a return statement returns None.

theory.heading: The mutable default argument trap
theory.body: Default values are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, not on every call. If the default is a mutable object such as a list, every call that relies on the default shares the same list, so data leaks between calls. The fix is to use None as a sentinel and create a new object inside the function.
points: Wrong: def add(item, bucket=[]).
Right: def add(item, bucket=None): bucket = [] if bucket is None else bucket.
The shared default is visible in add.__defaults__.

theory.heading: Scope: the LEGB rule
theory.body: When Python looks up a name it searches Local, then Enclosing function scopes, then Global (module), then Built-in. Assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local to that function for the whole body, which is why reading a global and then assigning to it raises UnboundLocalError. global rebinds a module-level name; nonlocal rebinds a name in the nearest enclosing function. Prefer returning values over mutating globals.
points: Local: names assigned inside the current function.
Enclosing: names in outer functions, used by closures.
Global: names at module top level.
Built-in: len, print, range and friends; shadowing them (list = [...]) is a common bug.

theory.heading: First-class functions, closures and lambdas
theory.body: Because functions are objects you can store them in a dictionary to build a dispatch table instead of a long if/elif chain, pass them as the key argument to sorted, or return them from a factory. A closure is created when an inner function references a variable of the outer function; the variable survives after the outer function returns. Closures are the foundation of decorators (Day 7). lambda creates a small anonymous function limited to a single expression.
points: sorted(users, key=lambda u: u['age']) passes a function as data.
Closures capture variables, not values: loop variables captured in lambdas all see the final value unless bound with a default (lambda i=i: i).
functools.partial pre-fills some arguments of a function.

theory.heading: Pass by object reference
theory.body: Python passes references to objects ('call by sharing'). The function receives a new name bound to the same object. Mutating a mutable argument (list.append) is visible to the caller, but rebinding the parameter (lst = [...]) is not. This explains both why functions can change a caller's list and why they cannot change a caller's int.
points: Mutation is visible outside; rebinding is not.
Copy defensively (list(arg), dict(arg)) if a function must not change its input.

example.title: A closure-based counter and the default-argument trap
example.body: make_counter returns an inner function that keeps its own count using nonlocal. The second part shows how a mutable default leaks state between calls and how the None sentinel fixes it.

code.source:
def make_counter(start=0):
    count = start
    def increment(step=1):
        nonlocal count
        count += step
        return count
    return increment

clicks = make_counter()
print(clicks(), clicks(), clicks(5))  # 1 2 7

def add_bad(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

def add_good(item, bucket=None):
    bucket = [] if bucket is None else bucket
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_bad('a'), add_bad('b'))    # ['a', 'b'] ['a', 'b']
print(add_good('a'), add_good('b'))  # ['a'] ['b']

interview.question: What are *args and **kwargs?
interview.answer: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. The same symbols in a call unpack a sequence or mapping into arguments.
interview.explanation: Show both directions (packing in the definition, unpacking in the call) and mention a real use such as wrapper functions in decorators.

interview.question: Why is def f(x, items=[]) dangerous?
interview.answer: The default list is created once when the function is defined and shared by every call that uses the default, so items appended in one call appear in the next. Use None as the default and create a new list inside.
interview.explanation: This is one of the most common Python interview questions. Explaining that defaults are evaluated at definition time is the key insight.

interview.question: Explain the LEGB rule. What do global and nonlocal do?
interview.answer: Python resolves names in Local, Enclosing, Global and Built-in scopes, in that order. global lets a function rebind a module-level name; nonlocal lets a nested function rebind a name in its enclosing function's scope.
interview.explanation: Mention UnboundLocalError: assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local everywhere in that function.

interview.question: Does Python pass arguments by value or by reference?
interview.answer: Neither exactly: it passes object references (call by sharing). The parameter is a new name for the same object, so in-place mutation of a mutable object is visible to the caller, while rebinding the parameter is not.
interview.explanation: A good answer gives a two-line example contrasting lst.append(1) with lst = [1].

interview.question: What is a closure and where is it used in practice?
interview.answer: A closure is an inner function that references variables from an enclosing function and keeps them alive after the outer function returns. Closures power decorators, callback factories, memoisation and configuration of handlers.
interview.explanation: Strong candidates mention the late-binding gotcha with lambdas in loops and that decorators are just closures applied with @ syntax.

lesson.title: Built-in Data Structures and Comprehensions
objectives: Choose between list, tuple, dict and set based on behaviour and time complexity.
Write list, dict and set comprehensions and generator expressions.
Use collections helpers such as Counter, defaultdict and deque.
Explain shallow versus deep copies of nested structures.
Sort complex data with key functions and multiple sort criteria.
lesson.definition: Python's built-in data structures are list (ordered, mutable sequence), tuple (ordered, immutable sequence), dict (insertion-ordered mapping of hashable keys to values, backed by a hash table) and set (unordered collection of unique hashable items). Comprehensions are concise expressions that build these collections from an iterable with optional filtering.

theory.heading: Lists and tuples
theory.body: A list is a dynamic array: indexing and append are O(1) (append is amortised), but inserting or deleting at the front is O(n) because elements must shift, and x in list is an O(n) scan. A tuple is an immutable sequence; because it cannot change it is hashable when its items are, so it can be a dict key, and it signals 'fixed record' to readers, for example a (lat, lng) pair or a database row.
points: list.append, list.pop() and indexing: O(1).
list.insert(0, x), list.pop(0) and x in list: O(n).
Tuple unpacking: name, age = row.
Use collections.deque for O(1) appends and pops at both ends (queues).

theory.heading: Dictionaries and sets
theory.body: dict and set are hash tables. Lookup, insertion and membership tests are O(1) on average, which is why converting a list to a set before many membership checks can turn an O(n*m) algorithm into O(n+m). Keys must be hashable. Since Python 3.7 dicts preserve insertion order as a language guarantee. Sets support mathematical operations: union |, intersection &, difference - and symmetric difference ^.
points: d.get(key, default) avoids KeyError for missing keys.
d.setdefault(key, []).append(v) groups values in one line.
d1 | d2 merges dictionaries (Python 3.9+); {**d1, **d2} works on older versions.
A set removes duplicates but does not keep order; dict.fromkeys(items) dedupes while keeping order.

theory.heading: Comprehensions and generator expressions
theory.body: A comprehension builds a collection in a single readable expression: [f(x) for x in items if cond(x)]. Dict comprehensions use {k: v for ...} and set comprehensions use {x for ...}. Using parentheses instead creates a generator expression, which produces items lazily without building a list in memory, ideal for sum(x * x for x in big_range). Keep comprehensions simple; nested logic belongs in a regular loop.
points: squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]
by_id = {u['id']: u for u in users}
Comprehension variables do not leak into the surrounding scope in Python 3.

theory.heading: The collections module
theory.body: Counter counts hashable items and has most_common(n). defaultdict creates a default value for missing keys, removing if-key-not-in-dict boilerplate. deque is a double-ended queue for BFS and sliding windows. namedtuple and dataclasses give lightweight records with named fields. Knowing these saves time in coding interviews and shows idiomatic Python.
points: Counter('banana') gives Counter({'a': 3, 'n': 2, 'b': 1}).
defaultdict(list) groups items; defaultdict(int) counts.
deque(maxlen=3) keeps only the last three items.

theory.heading: Copying and sorting
theory.body: Assignment never copies. list(x), x.copy() and x[:] make shallow copies: a new outer container whose items are the same objects, so nested lists are still shared. copy.deepcopy recursively copies nested objects. sorted() returns a new list and list.sort() sorts in place; both are stable and accept key= and reverse=. For multiple criteria return a tuple from the key, for example key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name) for score descending then name ascending.
points: Shallow copy: new container, shared items.
Deep copy: everything duplicated recursively.
Sorting is O(n log n) with Timsort and is stable.

demonstration.description: Compare a shallow and a deep copy of a nested list to see which changes are shared.

code.source:
import copy

grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = grid.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(grid)

grid[0].append(99)
print(shallow[0])  # shares inner lists
print(deep[0])     # independent
print({1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4}, {1, 2} | {5})

takeaways: Lists are dynamic arrays; front insertions and membership tests are O(n).
Dicts and sets are hash tables with average O(1) lookup; keys must be hashable.
Dicts keep insertion order since Python 3.7.
Comprehensions build collections; generator expressions produce items lazily.
Counter, defaultdict and deque remove a lot of boilerplate.
Shallow copies share nested objects; use deepcopy when you need full independence.

interview.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
interview.answer: A list is mutable and a tuple is immutable. Because of that a tuple of hashable items is hashable (usable as a dict key), slightly smaller and faster to create, and communicates a fixed-size record. Lists are for homogeneous collections that grow or change.
interview.explanation: Go beyond 'one is mutable': mention hashability and intent (records versus collections).

interview.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
interview.answer: A set is a hash table: Python hashes the value and jumps to its bucket, giving average O(1). A list must compare items one by one, which is O(n).
interview.explanation: Mention the practical trick of converting a list to a set before repeated membership tests, and that worst-case hash collisions degrade to O(n).

interview.question: Are Python dictionaries ordered?
interview.answer: Yes. Since Python 3.7 insertion order is guaranteed by the language specification (it was an implementation detail of CPython 3.6). Iteration returns keys in the order they were first inserted.
interview.explanation: Interviewers check whether your knowledge is current; mention OrderedDict still exists for move_to_end and order-sensitive equality.

interview.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
interview.answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but references the same inner objects. A deep copy recursively copies all nested objects, so changes to inner lists or dicts are not shared.
interview.explanation: Give the nested list example; this ties into bugs when copying configuration dicts or default data.

interview.question: How would you find the k most frequent words in a text, breaking ties alphabetically?

import sys
from collections import Counter

lines = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
k = int(lines[0])
text = ' '.join(lines[1:])

words = [w.strip('.,!?;:()').lower() for w in text.split()]
counts = Counter(w for w in words if w)

if not counts:
    print('No words')
else:
    print(f'Unique: {len(counts)}')
    ranked = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    for word, count in ranked[:k]:
        print(word, count)
explanation: Join all text lines so words on different lines are counted together.
Normalise each word with strip and lower in a list comprehension.
Counter counts the non-empty words in one pass.

lesson.title: Object-Oriented Python: Classes, Inheritance and Dunder Methods
objectives: Define classes with instance attributes, class attributes, methods and properties.
Use inheritance, method overriding and super() and explain the MRO.
Implement dunder methods such as __init__, __str__, __repr__, __eq__ and __lt__.
Distinguish instance methods, @classmethod and @staticmethod.
Apply polymorphism to remove type-checking if/elif chains.
lesson.definition: Object-oriented programming (OOP) organises code around objects that bundle data (attributes) with behaviour (methods). In Python a class is a blueprint created with the class keyword, an object is an instance of that class, and special 'dunder' (double underscore) methods let your objects plug into built-in syntax such as printing, comparison, len() and +.

theory.heading: Classes, instances and attributes
theory.body: __init__ initialises a new instance; self is the instance itself, passed automatically. Attributes assigned on self are per instance, while attributes defined in the class body are shared by all instances. A common bug is a mutable class attribute (items = []) that every instance accidentally shares. Python has no private keyword: a single underscore (_balance) means 'internal by convention' and a double underscore triggers name mangling to avoid clashes in subclasses.
points: Instance attribute: self.balance = 0 inside __init__.
Class attribute: interest_rate = 0.04 in the class body.
@property exposes a computed or validated attribute with attribute syntax.
__slots__ can restrict attributes and save memory for many small objects.

theory.heading: The four pillars in Python terms
theory.body: Encapsulation keeps state and the rules that change it together (a withdraw method that enforces a minimum balance). Abstraction exposes a simple interface and hides details; abc.ABC with @abstractmethod formalises it. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialise a parent class. Polymorphism means different classes respond to the same method call in their own way, so calling code does not need if type == ... branches. Python also embraces duck typing: if an object has the right methods, its class does not matter.
points: Encapsulation: methods guard invariants.
Abstraction: abstract base classes define required methods.
Inheritance: class Savings(Account).
Polymorphism: account.available() behaves differently per subclass.

theory.heading: Inheritance, super() and the MRO
theory.body: A subclass overrides a method by defining one with the same name, and super().method() calls the next implementation in the Method Resolution Order. Python supports multiple inheritance and resolves lookups with the C3 linearisation, visible through ClassName.__mro__. Django uses this heavily: class-based views combine mixins such as LoginRequiredMixin with ListView, and the order of base classes matters.
points: super().__init__(...) lets the parent initialise its part of the object.
Put mixins to the left of the main base class.
Favour composition over deep inheritance trees.

theory.heading: Dunder (magic) methods
theory.body: Dunder methods connect your class to Python's syntax and built-ins. __str__ gives a readable string for users (print), while __repr__ gives an unambiguous developer representation (the REPL, logs, containers). __eq__ defines ==; if you define __eq__ you must also define __hash__ (or the object becomes unhashable). __lt__ enables sorting; functools.total_ordering fills in the rest of the comparisons. __len__, __getitem__, __iter__, __contains__, __add__, __enter__/__exit__ and __call__ let objects behave like containers, numbers, context managers or functions.
points: print(obj) uses __str__, falling back to __repr__.
sorted(objs) needs __lt__.
Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None unless you define it.
@dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you.

theory.heading: Instance, class and static methods
theory.body: Instance methods receive self and work with one object. @classmethod receives the class (cls) and is used for alternative constructors such as User.from_dict(data), which also work correctly for subclasses. @staticmethod receives neither and is a plain function placed in the class namespace for organisation. Django model managers and form classes use all three patterns.
points: Alternative constructor: datetime.fromtimestamp is a classmethod.
Static method: a helper that does not need instance or class state.

example.title: A Money value object with dunder methods
example.body: Money stores amounts as integer paise, supports + and comparisons, has a readable __str__ and a debuggable __repr__, and stays hashable because equality and hash use the same fields.

interview.question: What is the difference between __str__ and __repr__?
interview.answer: __str__ returns a readable, user-facing string used by print() and str(). __repr__ returns an unambiguous developer-facing string, ideally one that could recreate the object, used by the REPL, logs and containers. If __str__ is missing Python falls back to __repr__.
interview.explanation: Mention that a list of objects prints each item's __repr__, which is why defining __repr__ helps debugging.

interview.question: What is the difference between @classmethod and @staticmethod?
interview.answer: A classmethod receives the class as cls and can create or inspect instances of that class or its subclasses, making it ideal for alternative constructors. A staticmethod receives neither self nor cls and is just a function grouped inside the class.
interview.explanation: An example like User.from_json(data) returning cls(...) shows why cls matters with inheritance.

interview.question: What does super() do, and what is the MRO?
interview.answer: super() returns a proxy that delegates method calls to the next class in the Method Resolution Order, the linearised list of base classes Python computes with C3. It makes cooperative multiple inheritance and mixins work.
interview.explanation: Relate it to Django mixins: class MyView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView) works because LoginRequiredMixin.dispatch calls super().dispatch().

interview.question: If you override __eq__ in a class, what happens to hashing?
interview.answer: Python sets __hash__ to None, so instances become unhashable and cannot be used in sets or as dict keys. If the object should be hashable, define __hash__ using the same immutable fields used for equality.
interview.explanation: This catches many candidates. Objects that are equal must have equal hashes; mutable objects usually should not be hashable.

interview.question: Explain polymorphism with an example from a web application.
interview.answer: Different classes implement the same interface, and the caller uses them interchangeably. For example, EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier and PushNotifier each implement send(user, message); the order service loops over configured notifiers and calls send without checking types.
interview.explanation: Concrete, domain-relevant examples score better than 'Dog and Cat both speak'. Mention duck typing as Python's flavour of polymorphism.

questions.topic: Functions, Arguments, Scope and Closures

questions.answer: The default list is created once when the function is defined and shared by every call that uses the default, so items appended in one call appear in the next. Use None as the default and create a new list inside.
questions.explanation: This is one of the most common Python interview questions. Explaining that defaults are evaluated at definition time is the key insight.

questions.topic: Functions, Arguments, Scope and Closures
questions.question: Explain the LEGB rule. What do global and nonlocal do?
questions.answer: Python resolves names in Local, Enclosing, Global and Built-in scopes, in that order. global lets a function rebind a module-level name; nonlocal lets a nested function rebind a name in its enclosing function's scope.
questions.explanation: Mention UnboundLocalError: assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local everywhere in that function.

questions.topic: Functions, Arguments, Scope and Closures
questions.question: Does Python pass arguments by value or by reference?
questions.answer: Neither exactly: it passes object references (call by sharing). The parameter is a new name for the same object, so in-place mutation of a mutable object is visible to the caller, while rebinding the parameter is not.
questions.explanation: A good answer gives a two-line example contrasting lst.append(1) with lst = [1].

questions.topic: Functions, Arguments, Scope and Closures
questions.question: What is a closure and where is it used in practice?
questions.answer: A closure is an inner function that references variables from an enclosing function and keeps them alive after the outer function returns. Closures power decorators, callback factories, memoisation and configuration of handlers.
questions.explanation: Strong candidates mention the late-binding gotcha with lambdas in loops and that decorators are just closures applied with @ syntax.

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures and Comprehensions
questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
questions.answer: A list is mutable and a tuple is immutable. Because of that a tuple of hashable items is hashable (usable as a dict key), slightly smaller and faster to create, and communicates a fixed-size record. Lists are for homogeneous collections that grow or change.
questions.explanation: Go beyond 'one is mutable': mention hashability and intent (records versus collections).

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures and Comprehensions
questions.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?

questions.explanation: Mention the practical trick of converting a list to a set before repeated membership tests, and that worst-case hash collisions degrade to O(n).

days.title: Object-Oriented Python: Classes, Inheritance and Dunder Methods
days.focus: Object-oriented programming (OOP) organises code around objects that bundle data (attributes) with behaviour (methods). In Python a class is a blueprint created with the class keyword, an object is an instance of that class, and special 'dunder' (double underscore) methods let your objects plug into built-in syntax such as printing, comparison, len() and +.
objectives: Define classes with instance attributes, class attributes, methods and properties.
Use inheritance, method overriding and super() and explain the MRO.
Implement dunder methods such as __init__, __str__, __repr__, __eq__ and __lt__.
Distinguish instance methods, @classmethod and @staticmethod.
Apply polymorphism to remove type-checking if/elif chains.
days.assignment: Simulate a small bank. A Savings account must keep at least 500 after a withdrawal. A Current account may go into overdraft down to -1000. Both start at 0. Commands: 'OPEN savings|current <owner>', 'DEPOSIT <owner> <amount>', 'WITHDRAW <owner> <amount>' and 'REPORT'. After a successful DEPOSIT or WITHDRAW print '<owner> balance: <balance>'. OPEN prints 'Opened <Kind> account for <owner>' where Kind is Savings or Current. REPORT prints every account as '<Kind> <owner>: <balance>' sorted by balance descending, keeping opening order for equal balances, or 'No accounts' if none exist. Errors print 'Error: <message>' with message 'account exists for <owner>', 'no account for <owner>', 'amount must be positive' or 'insufficient funds'.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: self is the instance; class attributes are shared by all instances.
Use super() so cooperative inheritance follows the MRO.
__str__ is for users, __repr__ is for developers.
Defining __eq__ requires defining __hash__ if objects must be hashable.
@classmethod is ideal for alternative constructors; @staticmethod for related helpers.
Polymorphism replaces type-checking branches with overridden methods.
